hook.line: In a barrio where every neighbour has a different version of the rumour, you need a short way to say that nobody agrees and everybody is entitled to their own.

examples.es: Cada una se fue a su casa.
examples.en: Each of the women went home.

examples.es: Cada quien sabe lo que hace.

rule:
*Cada quien* means "everyone, each one on their own". It is the usual Latin American way; *cada uno* works the same.

The verb is singular, even though the idea is many people: *cada quien tiene*, not *tienen*. English cheats with "their"; Spanish keeps one person: *su*.

For a group of women, use *cada una*: *Cada una se fue a su casa*. *Lo suyo* means "their own share".
smallPrint: Teachers call *cada* a distributive quantifier: it picks people out one at a time, so the verb agrees with one person.

readAndPick.es: Cada una se fue a su casa.
options: Each of the men went home.
Each of the women went home.
Each of them went to my house.

readAndPick.es: Cada quien sabe lo que hace.

options: Everyone pays for their own tinto.

readAndPick.es: Cada quien cuenta lo que vio.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *tiene* or *tienen* and type the whole sentence: *Cada quien ___ su versión.*
yourTurn.why: *Cada quien* is one person at a time, so the verb is singular.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Everyone pays for their own.
Type in Spanish: Everyone picks their own table.
Type in Spanish: Each of the women ordered a juice.
yourTurn.why: For a group of women, *cada* takes *una*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Everyone has their own story.
yourTurn.why: The short version needs no verb at all.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Everyone decides for themselves.
Change it for a group of women: *Cada uno se fue a su casa.* Say: Each of the women went home.
yourTurn.answer: Cada una se fue a su casa.
yourTurn.why: *Uno* becomes *una* when everyone in the group is a woman.

pitfalls.right: Cada una se fue a su casa.
